claims.text: Adding approximately 0.1 at.% carbon to a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote in situ formation of stable carbide phases.
The carbon can be uniformly incorporated into the alloy through a carburizing treatment during processing.
Carbon addition will trigger carbide formation under high-temperature service conditions.
Stable, finely dispersed Ta3C and Nb3C phases will form at or near the alloy surface.
The carbide phases will act as diffusion barriers that slow inward oxygen diffusion.
At high temperature, added carbon reacts with carbide-forming Ta and Nb to produce strongly bonded carbides.
The carbides reduce oxygen penetration and limit oxidation kinetics.
Reduced oxidation will preserve the alloy's microstructure and mechanical performance.
The proposed oxidation-resistance benefit should occur during a 10-hour exposure at 1000°C in ambient air or pure oxygen.
The carbon-doped alloy will have approximately 30% lower oxidation weight gain or oxide-scale thickness than the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy will oxidize faster and form thicker, potentially less-adherent oxide scales under identical conditions.
At significantly higher temperatures or different oxygen partial pressures, carbide stability and protective effectiveness may be compromised.
Prior work demonstrated Ta3C and Nb3C formation in a 0.1 at.% carbon-doped Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 RHEA under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions.
